lessons.title: Major Commercial Banana Varieties (Cavendish, Gros Michel, etc.)
lessons.body: When you grow bananas for money, the variety you choose decides your market, your yield, and your problems. The most planted commercial banana in Africa is Cavendish, also called Chinese banana or Williams. It produces large bunches of 15â25 kg, tolerates wind better than others, and is the main export type. But Cavendish is highly susceptible to Panama disease (Fusarium wilt) and black sigatoka. Gros Michel, known as 'Big Mike', was the export king before Panama disease wiped it out in the 1950s. It has thicker skin, better taste, and travels well, but it is almost impossible to grow commercially now because of Fusarium. In Africa, Gros Michel survives in backyard gardens and local markets. Other important varieties: Pisang Awak (also called Kayinja or Kiganda) is very hardy, resistant to sigatoka, and used for juice and beer in Uganda. Bluggoe (or Lujugira) is a cooking banana, important in East Africa. Plantain (Musa AAB) is a major staple in West and Central Africa, eaten cooked. Red bananas are sweeter and fetch premium prices in niche markets. For local markets, many farmers grow Sukali Ndizi (sugar banana) or Ndiizi, which is sweet and thin-skinned. For export, you need Cavendish clones like Grand Naine, Williams, and Dwarf Cavendish. Grand Naine is the most popular worldwide because it yields well and is shorter, making harvest easier. In Africa, the choice often depends on altitude: Cavendish does well from 0â1200 m, while highland cooking bananas (like East African Highland Bananas) thrive above 1200 m. Always match the variety to your local disease pressure, rainfall, and market demand. If you are near a city, sweet bananas and plantains sell fast. If you have a contract with an exporter, plant only certified Cavendish. Never plant a mix without checking what buyers want.

lessons.title: Selecting Varieties for Local Markets and Export
lessons.body: Your market decides your variety. For local markets in Africa, buyers want taste, size, and availability. Sweet bananas like Sukali Ndizi and Ndiizi are popular in Uganda, Kenya, and Tanzania. They are eaten fresh and sell in small bunches. Plantains (called 'gonja' in Uganda, 'ogede' in Nigeria) are essential for cooking and roasting; they fetch steady prices in West and Central Africa. Cooking bananas like East African Highland Bananas (Matooke) are the backbone of markets in Uganda, Rwanda, and Burundi. For these local markets, you can plant a mix of varieties to spread risk and harvest throughout the year. But for export, the rules are strict. Exporters demand Cavendish clonesâmainly Grand Naine, Williams, and Dwarf Cavendish. They want uniform bunches, 35â45 mm finger diameter, and no blemishes. You must have a guaranteed volume, usually at least 1 hectare, and follow GlobalG.A.P. standards. Export bananas are harvested green, packed in 18â20 kg boxes, and shipped at 13Â°C. If you are far from a port or airport, export is not for you. For local markets, you can sell at farm gate, roadside, or to traders. A good strategy: plant 70% of your land with a proven local variety (e.g., Matooke or plantain) and 30% with Cavendish for nearby urban markets. Always test a small plot of any new variety before planting the whole farm. Ask other farmers about yield, disease resistance, and market price. In Kenya, for example, farmers near Nairobi grow Cavendish for supermarkets and hotels. In Ghana, plantain farmers supply huge urban markets. Know your buyer before you plant.

lessons.title: Sources of Healthy Planting Material: Suckers, Tissue Culture
lessons.body: Banana planting material comes from two main sources: suckers and tissue culture plantlets. Suckers are shoots that grow from the mother plant's corm. They are cheap and easy to get, but they often carry diseases like Panama disease, banana bunchy top virus, and nematodes. There are two types of suckers: sword suckers (narrow leaves, good for planting) and water suckers (broad leaves, weak, poor yield). Always choose sword suckers from healthy, high-yielding mother plants. A good sword sucker is 30â50 cm tall, has a corm of at least 500 g, and has 3â5 healthy leaves. Never take suckers from a plant that looks sick or has produced small bunches. Tissue culture (TC) plantlets are grown in a laboratory from tiny pieces of healthy mother plants. They are disease-free, uniform, and produce higher yields. TC plantlets are sold in small bags or trays, usually 5â15 cm tall. They cost moreâabout $0.50 to $2 per plantletâbut you need fewer because they survive better. TC plantlets are the best choice if you are starting a commercial farm or if your soil has disease history. In Africa, TC labs exist in Kenya, Uganda, Nigeria, South Africa, and Ghana. You can also get them from certified nurseries. Suckers are still common for smallholders, but you must treat them. Soak suckers in hot water at 52â55Â°C for 20 minutes to kill nematodes and weevils. Then dip in a fungicide solution. For TC plantlets, handle gently: keep them in shade, water daily, and plant out after 6â8 weeks when they have 4â6 leaves. Never plant a sucker or TC plantlet that looks yellow, stunted, or has root damage.

lessons.title: Sucker Selection and Preparation
lessons.body: If you use suckers, you must select and prepare them carefully. Start by choosing mother plants that are healthy, have large bunches, and show no signs of disease. Look for sword suckersâthey have narrow, pointed leaves and a strong corm. Avoid water suckers: they have broad, round leaves and a weak connection to the mother. A good sword sucker is 30â50 cm tall, with a corm diameter of at least 10 cm and weight of 500 g or more. Use a sharp, clean machete or spade to cut the sucker from the mother corm. Make a clean cut, leaving a small piece of the mother corm attachedâthis helps the sucker establish. Do not damage the growing point. After cutting, trim the roots to about 5 cm and remove any damaged or diseased parts. Then treat the sucker to kill pests and diseases. The hot water treatment is simple: heat water to 52â55Â°C (use a thermometer), soak the cleaned suckers for 20 minutes, then cool them in clean water. This kills nematodes and banana weevils. Next, dip the corm in a fungicide solution, such as benomyl or thiabendazole, following label instructions. You can also dip in a slurry of wood ash and water to prevent fungal rot. After treatment, plant the suckers immediately in a nursery bed or directly in the field. If you must store them, keep them in a cool, shaded place for no more than 2 days. Plant in holes 40 cm x 40 cm x 40 cm, with the corm 5 cm below the soil surface. Water well. With good preparation, suckers can give you a harvest in 12â14 months. Poor suckers give small bunches or die. Always prepare more suckers than you needâabout 10% extraâto replace failures.

lessons.title: Tissue Culture Plantlets: Advantages and Handling
lessons.body: Tissue culture (TC) plantlets are the gold standard for commercial banana farming. They are produced in a laboratory from the growing tip of a healthy mother plant. Because they are grown in sterile conditions, they are free from Panama disease, bunchy top virus, and nematodes. TC plantlets are also uniform: every plant grows at the same rate, so you can harvest all at once. They yield 20â30% more than suckers and produce larger bunches. TC plantlets are small when you get themâusually 5â15 cm tall in a small bag or tray. They are delicate, so handle with care. When they arrive, keep them in a shaded nursery for 6â8 weeks. Water them daily, but do not soak the soil. Use a fine mist spray to avoid damaging leaves. After 2 weeks, start adding a weak liquid fertilizer (e.g., NPK 20-10-10 at 1 g per litre) once a week. By 6â8 weeks, they should have 4â6 leaves and be 20â30 cm tall. Then they are ready to plant in the field. Plant TC plantlets in the cool of the evening or on a cloudy day. Dig a hole 30 cm x 30 cm x 30 cm, place the plantlet with its root ball intact, and cover with soil. Water immediately. Keep the area weed-free and mulch around the plant. TC plantlets cost moreâ$0.50 to $2 eachâbut you need only 1,000â1,500 per hectare, compared to 1,200â1,800 suckers. The extra cost is recovered in higher yields and lower disease losses. In Africa, TC labs are in Kenya (e.g., KALRO), Uganda (NARO), Nigeria (IITA), and South Africa. Always buy from a certified lab or nursery. Never buy TC plantlets that are yellow, have distorted leaves, or are root-bound. With proper handling, TC plantlets give you a clean, profitable plantation.

lessons.title: Certification and Disease-Free Planting Material
lessons.body: Certification is your guarantee that planting material is healthy and true to type. In Africa, many countries have a national certification scheme for banana. For example, in Kenya, the Kenya Plant Health Inspectorate Service (KEPHIS) certifies tissue culture labs and nurseries. In Uganda, the National Agricultural Research Organisation (NARO) and the Ministry of Agriculture certify planting material. Certified material comes with a label or certificate showing the variety, the lab or nursery, and a batch number. It means the plants have been tested for diseases like Panama disease, bunchy top virus, and banana streak virus. Always ask for the certificate when you buy. If a seller cannot show certification, do not buyâespecially for tissue culture plantlets. For suckers, certification is rare, but you can still reduce risk by buying from a known healthy farm. Some cooperatives and NGOs run clean sucker multiplication plots. These are mother plants that have been tested and protected from disease. You can buy suckers from them with confidence. Never take suckers from a neighbour's farm without checking for disease. Panama disease can stay in the soil for decades, and once it enters your farm, you cannot remove it. The same applies to banana bunchy top virus, which is spread by aphids. Certified planting material costs 10â20% more, but it saves you from losing your entire plantation. In Africa, the Banana Breeding Program at IITA and the African Banana and Plantain Network promote certification. If you are starting a commercial farm, budget for certified TC plantlets. For smallholders, at least source suckers from a clean plot. Always keep records of where you bought your planting material. If disease appears, you can trace it back. Certification is not just a piece of paperâit is your insurance against crop failure.

quiz.q: Which banana variety was the main export type before Panama disease wiped it out in the 1950s?
quiz.explanation: Gros Michel was the dominant export banana until Fusarium wilt (Panama disease) destroyed plantations.

quiz.q: What is the most widely planted commercial Cavendish clone worldwide?
quiz.explanation: Grand Naine is the most popular due to high yield and shorter stature.

quiz.q: Which variety is known for being hardy and used for juice and beer in Uganda?
quiz.explanation: Pisang Awak, locally called Kayinja or Kiganda, is resistant to sigatoka and used for juice and beer.

quiz.q: For export, what finger diameter do buyers usually demand?
quiz.explanation: Export Cavendish bananas must have a finger diameter of 35â45 mm.

quiz.q: What is the recommended temperature for hot water treatment of suckers?
quiz.explanation: Soaking suckers at 52â55Â°C for 20 minutes kills nematodes and weevils without damaging the sucker.

quiz.q: Which type of sucker is best for planting?
quiz.explanation: Sword suckers have narrow leaves and a strong corm, giving better establishment and yield.

quiz.q: How long should tissue culture plantlets be kept in the nursery before field planting?
quiz.explanation: TC plantlets need 6â8 weeks in a shaded nursery to reach 4â6 leaves and 20â30 cm height.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of tissue culture plantlets over suckers?
quiz.explanation: TC plantlets are grown in sterile conditions, so they are free from Panama disease, bunchy top virus, and nematodes.

quiz.q: Which organization certifies tissue culture labs and nurseries in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: KEPHIS (Kenya Plant Health Inspectorate Service) is the certifying body in Kenya.

quiz.q: What is the recommended size of a planting hole for a tissue culture plantlet?
options: A) 20 cm x 20 cm x 20 cm
B) 30 cm x 30 cm x 30 cm
C) 40 cm x 40 cm x 40 cm
D) 50 cm x 50 cm x 50 cm
quiz.explanation: A 30 cm x 30 cm x 30 cm hole is sufficient for TC plantlets, while suckers may need 40 cm x 40 cm x 40 cm.

quiz.q: Which disease can stay in the soil for decades and cannot be removed once introduced?
quiz.explanation: Panama disease (Fusarium wilt) persists in soil for decades and has no cure.

quiz.q: What is the main market for plantains in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Plantains are a major staple, eaten cooked or roasted in West and Central Africa.

quiz.q: Which variety is known as 'Matooke' in Uganda?
quiz.explanation: East African Highland Bananas are cooking bananas called Matooke in Uganda.

quiz.q: What is the approximate cost of a tissue culture plantlet in Africa?
quiz.explanation: TC plantlets typically cost between $0.50 and $2.00 each, depending on the source and quantity.

quiz.q: How many suckers per hectare are typically needed for planting?
quiz.explanation: Banana planting density is usually 1,200â1,800 suckers per hectare, while TC plantlets need 1,000â1,500.

quiz.q: What should you do immediately after hot water treatment of suckers?
options: A) Store them in a cool place for a week
C) Plant them in full sun
D) Dry them in the sun
quiz.explanation: After hot water treatment, suckers should be dipped in a fungicide solution to prevent fungal rot.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of a good sword sucker?
quiz.explanation: Sword suckers have narrow, pointed leaves and a strong corm, unlike water suckers with broad leaves.

quiz.q: What is the main disadvantage of using suckers as planting material?
options: C) They are hard to find
D) They produce too many bunches
quiz.explanation: Suckers often carry diseases like Panama disease and nematodes, unlike tissue culture plantlets.

quiz.q: Which variety is a major staple in West and Central Africa?
quiz.explanation: Plantain (Musa AAB) is a staple food in West and Central Africa, eaten cooked.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for planting bananas?
quiz.explanation: A spacing of 3 m x 3 m is common for commercial bananas, giving about 1,100 plants per hectare.

quiz.q: What does certification of planting material guarantee?
quiz.explanation: Certification ensures the material is free from specified diseases and is the correct variety.

quiz.q: Which pest is controlled by hot water treatment of suckers?
quiz.explanation: Hot water treatment at 52â55Â°C kills banana weevils and nematodes in suckers.

quiz.q: What is the first step in preparing a sucker for planting?
options: B) Cut from mother plant with a clean tool
quiz.explanation: The first step is to cut a healthy sword sucker from the mother plant using a clean, sharp tool.

quiz.q: Which African country has a tissue culture lab run by NARO?
quiz.explanation: NARO (National Agricultural Research Organisation) operates tissue culture labs in Uganda.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of tissue culture plantlets regarding harvest?
options: A) They can be harvested year-round
quiz.explanation: TC plantlets are uniform, so they mature at the same time, allowing once-off harvest.

quiz.q: Which market would you target if you grow Grand Naine?
quiz.explanation: Grand Naine is a Cavendish clone, the preferred type for export markets.

quiz.q: What is a recommended practice when buying tissue culture plantlets?
options: A) Buy from any roadside seller
B) Buy from certified labs or nurseries
D) Buy plants with yellow leaves
quiz.explanation: Certified labs or nurseries guarantee disease-free, true-to-type plantlets.

quiz.q: How long can you store treated suckers before planting?
quiz.explanation: Treated suckers should be planted immediately or stored in a cool, shaded place for no more than 2 days.

quiz.q: Which variety is known for sweet, thin-skinned fruit popular in local markets?
quiz.explanation: Sukali Ndizi (sugar banana) is sweet and thin-skinned, sold fresh in local markets.

quiz.q: What is the role of KEPHIS in banana farming?
quiz.explanation: KEPHIS certifies tissue culture labs and nurseries to ensure healthy planting material in Kenya.
